title: Russian Federation, State Duma Elections, 19 September 2021: Needs Assessment Mission Report
publisher: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
claim: The OSCE mission said approved constitutional changes enabled the incumbent president to run for two more terms, extended presidential powers over judges, and recent legal changes further limited standing, assemblies, foreign agents, media, and internet regulation; interlocutors said the amendments were tailored to limit competition.
source_confidence_reason: Direct OSCE election-observation reporting with specific legal and political findings from contemporaneous interlocutors.
period_fit: Inherited baseline entering 2022; directly relevant to the 2022 political-freedom environment.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Putin’s presidency and the broader Kremlin-controlled electoral framework; the report directly names the incumbent president benefit and executive/legal changes.
contrary_evidence: State institutions told ODIHR the framework would ensure genuine competition and respect the rule of law.

title: No OSCE observers for Russian parliamentary elections following major limitations
publisher: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
claim: The OSCE said Russian authorities imposed limitations that prevented an independent observer mission, severely restricting the number of observers and undermining effective and credible election observation.
source_confidence_reason: Direct OSCE statement about host-state restrictions on independent observation.
period_fit: Inherited baseline entering 2022; relevant to the electoral environment that carried into 2022.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to the Russian authorities under Putin, which controlled the observation access and election conditions.
contrary_evidence: The authorities cited sanitary-epidemiological concerns as the reason for the restrictions.

title: Putin approves changes allowing him to stay in power until 2036 By Reuters
claim: Reuters reported that Putin opened the door to constitutional changes that would let him remain in power until 2036 by resetting his presidential term tally to zero.
source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a public parliamentary speech and constitutional trajectory, but hosted on a syndication platform.
period_fit: Inherited baseline shaping 2022 authority and succession expectations.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin because he personally backed the constitutional reset in parliament.
contrary_evidence: Putin said he favored term limits once Russia became politically mature and framed the move as a stability issue.

title: Doc. 15827: compendium of written amendments (Final version)
publisher: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe
claim: PACE said the abolition of presidential term limits for Putin violated constitutional and international principles and that the concentration of presidential power, together with weak checks and balances, had turned Russia into a de facto dictatorship.
source_confidence_reason: Official parliamentary text summarizing constitutional and democratic concerns, though adopted after the target year.
period_fit: Retrospective on the 2020-2022 constitutional trajectory relevant to 2022 governance.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Putin’s regime and the incumbent-benefiting constitutional changes.
contrary_evidence: This is a later Assembly text, not a contemporaneous 2022 finding.

title: Russian Federation: Authorities impose censorship on media and crush peaceful anti-war protests following invasion of Ukraine
claim: Roskomnadzor ordered media to rely only on official Russian sources for invasion coverage and threatened sanctions for spreading false information, effectively imposing censorship.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights organization statement with specific legal and regulatory details.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin’s state apparatus because Roskomnadzor acted as the official media watchdog under his government.
contrary_evidence: Russian authorities framed the measure as preventing false information about the war.

title: Russia: Kremlin’s ruthless crackdown stifles independent journalism and anti-war movement
claim: Amnesty said Russian authorities blocked independent media, banned Facebook and Twitter, and had arbitrarily arrested more than 13,800 people at anti-war rallies since 24 February 2022.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous NGO reporting with concrete arrest and censorship figures.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin’s government because the crackdown was implemented by state authorities and Roskomnadzor/police.
contrary_evidence: Authorities described the war and restrictions as necessary responses to the invasion and misinformation.

title: Russia: Arbitrary Detentions of Anti-War Protesters
claim: HRW said Russian authorities arbitrarily detained at least 5,982 anti-war protesters across Russia between February 24 and 28 and threatened media outlets with blocking if their reporting differed from the official narrative.
locator: Update paragraph with OVD-Info figures and opening summary
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous HRW reporting that cites an independent monitor and describes state conduct directly.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Russian authorities under Putin through police and media-regulator actions.
contrary_evidence: Authorities warned that unsanctioned protests and support for foreign organizations could be prosecuted as security threats.

title: Russia: Brutal Arrests and Torture, Ill-Treatment of Anti-War Protesters
claim: HRW reported that police detained protesters brutally and that the ban on public gatherings remained in force, showing coercive suppression of peaceful protest after the invasion.
locator: Update lines around March 13 and opening summary
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous rights reporting with specific protest-detention examples and an official legal context.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Putin’s government because police and public-order rules were used to suppress dissent.
contrary_evidence: Russian officials treated the protests as unsanctioned and maintained COVID/public-order restrictions.

title: Russians dare to protest war; AP dares to report it
claim: AP reported that Russia’s draconian fake-news law made fair, accurate, critical reporting almost impossible and that protesters were being charged for tiny anti-war signs and slogans.
source_confidence_reason: AP’s reporting is firsthand, specific, and contemporaneous, though it is a secondary media source.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to the Putin government because the prosecutions and chilling effect flowed from the new legal regime and police enforcement.
contrary_evidence: The state portrayed the law as necessary to stop false claims about the military and war.

title: Repressions in Russia in 2022
claim: OVD-Info said Russia began internal repression on an unprecedented scale in 2022, with more than 21,000 arrests, at least 370 criminal defendants for anti-war speech, more than 200,000 blocked internet resources, and 11 treason sentences.
source_confidence_reason: Major independent Russian monitoring project with specific year-end counts and direct reporting methodology.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Russian state authorities under Putin because the figures describe arrests, prosecutions, and blocking carried out by the state.
contrary_evidence: The report includes a broad range of protests beyond anti-war actions and is an advocacy-monitoring product.

title: Репрессии в России в 2022 году
claim: OVD-Info reported 19,478 anti-war detentions since February 24, the use of conscription notices at mobilization protests, preventive detentions via facial recognition, and repeated police violence against protesters.
source_confidence_reason: Local-language annual monitor with concrete year-specific counts and detailed mechanisms of coercion.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Russian state authorities under Putin because the practices are described as police and security-service conduct in 2022.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes other non-anti-war protests, which shows the repression was broader than one issue area.

title: Russia: Authorities close down Amnesty International’s Moscow Office
claim: Russian authorities shut down Amnesty International’s Moscow office and also closed or delisted other international NGOs, while blocking Amnesty’s Russian-language website.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous NGO statement about direct state action against civil society organizations.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin’s government through the Ministry of Justice and media regulator actions.
contrary_evidence: The ministry said the offices had legal violations.

title: Russian journalists are being silenced to stifle reporting of protests
claim: Amnesty said Russian authorities used a sophisticated system of restrictions and severe reprisals to crush public protests and suppress reporting by journalists and independent monitors.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous reporting tied to a focused new report on protest monitoring and reprisals.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to the Putin government because the report describes state reprisals and law-enforcement conduct.
contrary_evidence: Authorities justified restrictions as law enforcement and public-order measures.

title: Human Rights Committee Considers Report of the Russian Federation in the Absence of a Delegation, Experts Raise Issues on the Persecution of Journalists and the Arrests of Protesters
claim: UN experts said there were thousands of cases of harassment and persecution of journalists, hundreds of Russian journalists had been detained for reporting on the war or protests, and there had been mass arrests in response to peaceful demonstrations.
source_confidence_reason: UN meeting summary of an official treaty-body review with multiple expert interventions.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Russian state authorities under Putin because the committee described state detention and harassment of journalists and protesters.
contrary_evidence: The Russian Federation did not send a delegation, so the review could not include an on-the-record state rebuttal.

title: We publish a report on political prisoners and political repression in Russia in 2022
claim: Memorial said repression of public dissent reached unprecedented levels in 2022, political opposition was effectively outlawed, independent media were shut down, censorship was institutionalized, protest activity was suppressed, and the number of political prisoners reached 513 by the end of 2022.
source_confidence_reason: Major Russian rights project summarizing its own monitored casework and year-end counts.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin’s regime because the report describes state repression, censorship, and police-force conduct in 2022.
contrary_evidence: This is an advocacy-monitoring report and is retrospective rather than contemporaneous.

title: Политзаключённые и политические репрессии в России в 2022 году
claim: Memorial said 2022 was marked by de facto military censorship, 74 new names were added to the main political-prisoner list, and more than 5,000 administrative cases and 200-plus criminal cases targeted anti-army speech.
source_confidence_reason: Local-language retrospective report with explicit annual statistics and repression categories.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin’s regime because the report describes state repression in response to anti-war speech and public dissent.
contrary_evidence: The report is a retrospective summary and not a contemporaneous government record.

title: Putin signs law expanding Russia's rules against 'LGBT propaganda'
claim: Reuters-reported coverage said Putin signed a law expanding Russia’s LGBT propaganda restrictions so broadly that it effectively outlawed any public expression of LGBT behaviour or lifestyle and could penalize positive or neutral information online and in media.
source_confidence_reason: Reuters-based secondary reporting on a signed law and its stated scope.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin because he signed the law and it was enacted by his state.
contrary_evidence: The Kremlin framed the law as protecting traditional values.

title: Russia
claim: RSF says that since Russia’s large-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, almost all independent media have been banned, blocked, or declared foreign agents or undesirable organizations, and that all others are subject to military censorship.
source_confidence_reason: RSF country page is current but explicitly summarizes the post-2022 media environment in Russia.
period_fit: Retrospective summary of the 2022 media regime carried into the chapter period.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Putin’s government and wartime censorship apparatus.
contrary_evidence: This is a current summary page rather than a 2022-dated report.

title: World Report 2023: Russian Federation
claim: HRW said that in 2022 Russian authorities launched an all-out drive to eradicate public dissent, introduced war-censorship laws with long prison sentences, and expanded the foreign-agents regime while suppressing political speech.
source_confidence_reason: Annual country chapter summarizing multiple 2022 mechanisms of repression and censorship.
ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to Putin’s government because the laws and prosecutions were enacted and enforced by the state.
contrary_evidence: The chapter also notes that some repression trends predated 2022, so not all deterioration is unique to that year.

title: Data on politically motivated criminal persecutions in Russia
claim: OVD-Info states that it monitors politically motivated criminal cases daily, compiles a public database, and sources cases from court websites, Russian media, direct testimony, relatives, lawyers, and other rights groups.
source_confidence_reason: Methodology page describing the monitoring system behind the statistics used elsewhere in the dossier.
period_fit: Cross-cutting source-family reliability for the 2022 repression evidence.
ruler_attribution: This does not directly attribute conduct to Putin; it supports the reliability of the OVD-Info evidence family.
contrary_evidence: This is methodological rather than conduct evidence.

title: Elections in Russian Federation
publisher: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
claim: The OSCE elections portal shows that Russia’s election-observation record includes only limited and heavily constrained missions after 2021, underscoring the narrow international scrutiny available around the chapter period.
locator: Page listing of Russia election missions and reports
source_confidence_reason: Metadata page rather than a substantive report, but useful for mission history and coverage context.
period_fit: Inherited baseline and observation-coverage context for 2022.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to the Putin-era election environment, but only as background context.
contrary_evidence: The page itself is a mission index, not a findings document.

title: Annexation of Ukrainian territories is illegal and a threat to human rights, say OSCE human rights Director and OSCE media freedom Representative
publisher: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
claim: The OSCE said Russia's illegal annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, signed into law earlier that week, followed illegal so-called referenda in occupied Ukrainian territory and further aggravated the human-rights situation.
source_confidence_reason: Official OSCE press release with direct, date-specific findings about the annexation and its legal status.
ruler_attribution: High: the annexation was a Kremlin act under Putin's authority.
contrary_evidence: Russia claimed the annexation and referenda were lawful expressions of self-determination.

title: Russia/Ukraine: Illegitimate results of sham 'referenda' must not enable illegal annexation of occupied areas
claim: Amnesty said Russia's occupied-territory referenda were held at gunpoint in the presence of Russian soldiers and proxies, with fabricated turnout and results, and were illegal under international law.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous human-rights reporting with specific mechanism and timing; strong on coercion though based on field reporting and social-media/media accounts.
ruler_attribution: High: the referenda and annexation drive were carried out by Russian authorities and occupation structures under Putin's command.
contrary_evidence: Russia portrayed the votes as legitimate self-determination and Ukraine rejected them outright.

title: 2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Ukraine - Russia-Occupied Areas
claim: The report says Russia adopted legal acts extending Russian legislation to Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhya on September 30, required residents to be recognized as Russian citizens unless they refused, and on October 19 Putin imposed martial law with curfews, property seizures, internment, and restrictions on movement, assembly, and political parties.
source_confidence_reason: Official country-report language summarizing dated Russian legal acts and Putin's decree; strong for the formal control mechanism in occupied areas.
ruler_attribution: High: the legal extension of rule and martial-law decree are attributable to Putin and his government.
contrary_evidence: Russia treated the occupied regions as Russian territory and justified the measures as lawful administration.

title: Crimea: Freedom in the World 2022 Country Report
claim: Freedom House reported that occupation authorities compelled residents to accept Russian citizenship and surrender Ukrainian passports, and that as many as 4,700 people had been forcibly deported since the beginning of the occupation.
source_confidence_reason: Established annual Freedom House country report; strong independent baseline on coercive political control in occupied Crimea, though not a direct transcript of a Putin order.
period_fit: Ongoing 2022 occupation conditions reported in the 2022 country report.
ruler_attribution: Moderate to high: these coercive citizenship and deportation practices were carried out under the Russian occupation regime aligned to Putin's rule.
contrary_evidence: Russia continued to deny the illegality of the annexation and framed the measures as normal state administration.

title: Russia Instructs Teachers to Spread Disinformation About Ukraine
claim: HRW said Russia's Education Ministry told teachers to read a script and screen a video of Putin presenting the invasion as freedom and a peaceful anti-genocide measure, while warning that teachers who dissent could be fired and that criticism of the war could bring up to 15 years in prison.
source_confidence_reason: Direct contemporaneous rights reporting with specific quoted script language and concrete sanctions for dissent; strong evidence of state propaganda and coercion in civic space.
ruler_attribution: High: the propaganda script came from the Education Ministry and centered on Putin's own public justification for war.
contrary_evidence: The ministry claimed the lesson was a factual civic-education session and denied coercive intent.
